analysis.title: Why volatility may reinforce the commodity case (UBS House View - Daily Asia)
key_insights: UBS CIO says renewed volatility does not weaken the strategic case for commodities. It argues the asset class's differentiated outlooks and return drivers could strengthen portfolio resilience.
Markets are reassessing two assumptions besides the AI trade debate: that Middle East tensions are easing, and that the Fed's tightening cycle is nearing an end.

Brent briefly fell below USD 90 on Tuesday, a two-month low, on more constructive White House comments about possible talks with Iran. It rebounded to about USD 93 after Iran denied direct talks and further attacks on vessels near the Strait of Hormuz were reported.

A stronger-than-expected October US inflation reading and hawkish Fed comments moved market pricing back toward further rate hikes. Higher Treasury yields and a stronger US dollar sent gold down nearly 3% on Tuesday to about USD 3,981 an ounce.

Oil supply buffers remain limited. Global visible oil inventories were 7.8 billion barrels at end-September, more than 500 million barrels below pre-war February levels, and most pledged strategic reserve releases are complete.

Record freight costs and constrained tanker capacity mean transport availability, not only production, is setting the delivered cost of crude. UBS thinks current prices are too low relative to the supply outlook.
UBS expects Brent to reach USD 110 a barrel by year-end and keeps a moderately constructive near-term crude outlook, while noting unusually high forecast uncertainty.

Gold: elevated real yields and a firm dollar may keep it volatile near term. Structural support comes from Q3 central bank purchases up 42% y/y to 321 metric tons (World Gold Council) and ETF inflows of 211 metric tons that lifted global holdings to a record above 4,250 metric tons.
UBS suggests underallocated investors consider adding gold exposure on pullbacks below USD 4,000 an ounce, and views gold as a strategic diversifier.

Copper is UBS's preferred industrial metal, backed by power grid, data center, electrification and AI infrastructure investment. The EIA expects US electricity consumption to rise about 3.7% between 2025 and 2027.

Copper supply is tight. September output at two key Chilean operations fell 21% and 14% y/y, and Shanghai Futures Exchange-monitored stocks fell more than 24% in the latest weekly data to their lowest since January 2024.

UBS favors actively managed commodity strategies with diversified exposure across precious metals, energy, industrial metals and agriculture, citing low historical correlation with equities and bonds.

sector_views.rationale: Low correlation with equities and bonds gives structural return and diversification. UBS favors actively managed, diversified strategies across precious metals, energy, industrial metals and agriculture.
Inventories are well below pre-war levels, reserve releases are largely done, and Hormuz shipping and freight constraints limit supply. UBS sees current prices as too low.
Copper is the preferred industrial metal. Power grid, data center and AI infrastructure demand meets constrained Chilean output and falling Chinese inventories.
Near-term volatility from real yields and the dollar, offset by central bank and ETF demand. UBS suggests adding on pullbacks below USD 4,000 an ounce.

tension_points.bull_case: Limited oil buffers, record central bank and ETF gold demand, and tight copper supply support commodities. UBS expects Brent at USD 110 by year-end.
tension_points.bear_case: A hawkish Fed with higher yields and a stronger dollar pressures gold, and US-Iran talks could pull oil lower, as Brent's dip below USD 90 showed.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Gold holding below USD 4,000 an ounce is the level UBS flags for adding exposure, so it marks where the pullback entry opens.
